papers.title: Transformer-Based Neural Architecture Search for Edge Computing Environments
papers.abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) has emerged as a promising approach to automate the design of deep learning models, yet existing methods remain computationally prohibitive for resource-constrained edge devices. In this work, we present EdgeNAS, a transformer-based framework that leverages attention mechanisms to efficiently explore the architecture search space while simultaneously optimizing for latency, energy consumption, and accuracy on edge hardware. We introduce a novel multi-objective fitness function that Pareto-optimizes across these constraints and propose a differentiable search strategy that reduces search time by 78% compared to state-of-the-art methods. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and a proprietary IoT sensor dataset demonstrate that EdgeNAS discovers architectures achieving 94.3% accuracy on edge TPUs with 3.2ms inference latency, outperforming manually designed networks and prior NAS approaches. We further validate our method through deployment on NVIDIA Jetson Nano and Raspberry Pi 4 platforms, confirming real-world efficacy. Our findings suggest that transformer-guided search represents a scalable, generalizable paradigm for automated edge AI design.
papers.journal: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology

papers.title: Quantum Error Correction Using Topological Codes in Noisy Intermediate-Scale Devices
papers.abstract: The realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation hinges on effective error correction strategies capable of operating within the decoherence constraints of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. This paper presents a comprehensive study of surface code and color code implementations on superconducting qubit arrays, with particular focus on decoding latency and threshold error rates achievable on current hardware generations. We introduce a machine learning-augmented minimum-weight perfect matching (ML-MWPM) decoder that reduces decoding time by 62% while maintaining logical error rates below 10^-6 at physical error rates of 0.3%. Numerical simulations using a realistic noise model incorporating crosstalk, leakage, and measurement errors are validated against experimental results on a 72-qubit processor. Our results indicate that topological codes, combined with hardware-aware decoder optimization, represent the most viable near-term pathway to quantum advantage in error-corrected settings. We discuss implications for quantum memory lifetimes and the road to universal fault-tolerant quantum computation.

papers.title: CRISPR-Cas13 Mediated RNA Knockdown in Glioblastoma: Targeting the EGFR-PTEN Axis
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) remains among the most lethal human cancers, with a median survival of 15 months despite aggressive multimodal therapy. Dysregulation of the EGFR-PTEN signaling axis is a hallmark of GBM pathogenesis, rendering it a compelling therapeutic target. Here, we harness CRISPR-Cas13d, a programmable RNA-targeting nuclease, to achieve sequence-specific knockdown of EGFR mRNA in patient-derived GBM organoids and an orthotopic mouse model. We designed and screened 48 guide RNAs (gRNAs) targeting diverse EGFR transcript regions, identifying a lead candidate achieving 94% knockdown efficiency with minimal collateral transcriptome disruption as assessed by bulk RNA sequencing. Treatment with Cas13d-EGFR constructs delivered via lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) reduced organoid viability by 81% and extended median survival in tumor-bearing mice from 22 to 41 days. Combination with temozolomide (TMZ) further extended survival to 63 days. Off-target analyses across 12,000 predicted sites revealed no significant mis-targeting events. These findings establish CRISPR-Cas13d as a potent, specific platform for RNA-level oncogene silencing in GBM and support its advancement toward clinical translation.

papers.title: Federated Learning with Differential Privacy for Clinical Data Sharing Across Hospital Networks
papers.abstract: Collaborative machine learning across healthcare institutions holds enormous promise for improving diagnostic models, yet patient privacy regulations and institutional data silos present significant barriers. We propose FedMedDP, a federated learning framework augmented with local differential privacy (LDP) that enables hospitals to collaboratively train deep learning models on electronic health records (EHR) without sharing raw patient data. Our approach integrates a novel adaptive noise mechanism that dynamically calibrates privacy budgets per data stratum based on sensitivity analysis, preserving model utility while guaranteeing (ε, δ)-differential privacy with ε = 1.2 and δ = 10^-5. Evaluated on the MIMIC-IV dataset partitioned across 8 simulated hospital nodes, FedMedDP achieves 91.4% AUROC for 30-day readmission prediction—within 2.1% of a centralized non-private baseline—while reducing communication overhead by 34% through gradient compression. A real-world pilot involving 4 academic medical centers demonstrated robust performance on sepsis onset detection (AUROC 0.89) with full HIPAA compliance. Our work bridges the gap between privacy-preserving computation and clinically actionable predictive modeling.

papers.title: On the Convergence of Stochastic Gradient Descent with Adaptive Momentum in Non-Convex Landscapes
papers.abstract: Understanding the convergence behavior of adaptive gradient methods in non-convex optimization settings remains an open challenge in machine learning theory. In this paper, we provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of AdaGrad-Momentum, a variant combining adaptive per-parameter learning rates with heavy-ball momentum, in the context of non-convex stochastic optimization. We prove that AdaGrad-Momentum achieves an O(1/√T) convergence rate to first-order stationary points under mild smoothness and bounded variance assumptions, matching the best known rates for SGD while offering superior empirical performance on ill-conditioned loss surfaces. Furthermore, we derive tight lower bounds showing that no first-order method can surpass this rate in the general non-convex stochastic setting. We supplement our theoretical findings with extensive numerical experiments on ResNet-50 training on ImageNet and BERT fine-tuning on GLUE benchmarks, demonstrating 15–22% faster wall-clock convergence compared to Adam and AdamW baselines. These results shed light on the theoretical foundations underpinning modern deep learning optimizers and suggest principled modifications to improve their practical efficiency.

papers.title: Perovskite-Silicon Tandem Solar Cells Exceeding 33% Efficiency via Interface Passivation Engineering
papers.abstract: Monolithic perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells represent a transformative opportunity to surpass the Shockley-Queisser efficiency limit of single-junction photovoltaics. Despite rapid advances, non-radiative recombination at perovskite grain boundaries and heterojunction interfaces remains the primary efficiency bottleneck. We report a holistic interface passivation strategy employing self-assembled molecular monolayers (SAMs) functionalized with carboxylate and phosphonate anchoring groups at both the hole-transport layer (HTL)/perovskite and perovskite/electron-transport layer (ETL) interfaces. The optimized device architecture achieves a certified power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 33.4% under AM1.5G illumination, with an open-circuit voltage of 1.91 V approaching the radiative limit. Stability testing per ISOS-L-2 protocols demonstrates 95% retention of initial efficiency after 1,000 hours of continuous illumination at 85°C. Optical modeling and transient photovoltage decay measurements confirm that passivation reduces interface defect density by two orders of magnitude. Our results establish a scalable, process-compatible pathway to commercialization of high-efficiency tandem photovoltaics.

papers.title: Social Media Echo Chambers and Political Polarization: A Longitudinal Network Analysis
papers.abstract: The relationship between social media algorithmic curation and political polarization has attracted significant scholarly attention, yet causal evidence linking platform-induced echo chambers to offline attitude change remains scarce. We conduct a longitudinal network analysis spanning 48 months (2020–2024) on a panel of 210,000 Twitter/X users, tracking network homophily, cross-partisan exposure, and self-reported political attitudes via biannual surveys. Using a difference-in-differences design exploiting the natural experiment of Twitter's 2022 algorithmic timeline changes, we find that increased algorithmic amplification of in-group content raises affective polarization by 0.34 standard deviations over 12 months while reducing cross-cutting exposure by 41%. Critically, we document heterogeneous effects: users with high pre-existing ideological commitment exhibit stronger polarization responses, while politically moderate users show resilience to echo chamber formation. Our findings have direct implications for platform design regulation and underscore the importance of exposure diversity metrics as policy levers for democratic health.

papers.title: Mechanistic Insights into SARS-CoV-2 Omicron Subvariant Immune Evasion via Spike Protein Conformational Dynamics
papers.abstract: Successive Omicron subvariants of SARS-CoV-2 have demonstrated remarkable capacity to evade both vaccine-induced and infection-acquired immunity through mutations concentrated in the spike protein receptor-binding domain (RBD). To elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying this evasion, we performed microsecond-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the BA.2.86 and JN.1 spike trimers in complex with key neutralizing antibodies from the COVOX-159 and S309 panels. Our simulations reveal that a cluster of mutations (K356T, R346T, F456L) induces conformational redistribution of the RBD, reducing antibody-accessible epitopes by 38% while paradoxically enhancing ACE2 binding affinity by 1.7-fold through allosteric stabilization of the 'up' conformation. Free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations corroborate these findings and identify a previously uncharacterized allosteric site as a potential broad-spectrum antiviral target. Experimental validation via cryo-EM and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) assays confirms key mechanistic predictions. These results provide a structural framework for next-generation pan-sarbecovirus vaccine and therapeutic design.

papers.title: Enantioselective Synthesis of Quaternary Carbon Centers via Asymmetric Nickel-Catalyzed Conjunctive Cross-Coupling
papers.abstract: The construction of all-carbon quaternary stereocenters through catalytic asymmetric methods represents one of the foremost challenges in modern synthetic chemistry. Existing approaches are constrained by substrate scope limitations, harsh reaction conditions, or reliance on precious metal catalysts. Herein, we disclose an asymmetric nickel(0)-catalyzed conjunctive cross-coupling of tertiary alkyl halides, vinyl zinc reagents, and aryl boronic acids that assembles quaternary carbon centers with high enantioselectivity (er up to 97:3) and diastereoselectivity (dr up to >20:1) under mild conditions (23°C, ambient atmosphere). Mechanistic investigations using radical clock probes, EPR spectroscopy, and DFT calculations are consistent with a Ni(0)/Ni(I)/Ni(III) catalytic cycle involving enantio-determining radical recombination at a chiral Ni(III) intermediate. The reaction tolerates a broad array of functional groups including esters, nitriles, protected amines, and heterocycles, enabling late-stage diversification of complex pharmaceutical intermediates. Application to the asymmetric total synthesis of (+)-eurotinone is demonstrated in 8 steps from commercially available materials.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

papers.title: Postcolonial Architectures of Memory: Heritage Contestation in West African Urban Spaces
papers.abstract: Urban heritage sites in West Africa occupy contested terrain, serving simultaneously as loci of colonial memory, national identity construction, and tourist commodification. Drawing on 18 months of ethnographic fieldwork in Accra, Dakar, and Lagos—complemented by archival analysis of colonial administrative records and interviews with 214 residents, heritage administrators, and urban planners—this study examines how postcolonial governments, civil society actors, and diasporic communities negotiate the meaning and material transformation of former colonial edifices. Theorizing through a framework that synthesizes memory studies, postcolonial urbanism, and assemblage theory, we trace how contested heritage becomes a site of ongoing, multidirectional memory work rather than a fixed repository of the past. Our findings reveal that community-led heritage reinterpretation initiatives, when institutionally supported, generate more durable and equitable outcomes than top-down preservation mandates. We further argue that the concept of 'reparative heritage' offers a productive analytical lens for understanding how formerly colonized societies navigate the tension between historical acknowledgment and future-oriented urban development.

papers.title: Graph Neural Networks for Protein-Protein Interaction Prediction at Proteome Scale
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) govern virtually all cellular processes, and mapping the human interactome has profound implications for understanding disease mechanisms and identifying therapeutic targets. High-throughput experimental methods remain costly and incomplete, motivating computational PPI prediction approaches. We present ProteGraph, a heterogeneous graph neural network framework that integrates structural, sequence, and co-evolutionary features within a unified message-passing architecture to predict binary PPIs and binding affinities at proteome scale. ProteGraph is pretrained on AlphaFold2 structural predictions for 20,000 human proteins and fine-tuned on curated interaction data from STRING v12, BioGRID, and IntAct. On held-out test sets, it achieves AUROC of 0.947 for binary interaction prediction and Pearson r = 0.81 for binding affinity estimation—improvements of 12.3% and 18.6% over the best published baselines respectively. We apply ProteGraph to generate the first comprehensive in silico human interactome map spanning 87,000 predicted high-confidence interactions, revealing 1,240 previously unreported interactions with strong experimental validation rates in follow-up yeast two-hybrid assays (62% confirmation). A web server and pre-computed interaction database are publicly available.

papers.title: Microplastic Contamination in Deep-Sea Sediments: Abundance, Distribution, and Polymer Characterization
papers.abstract: Microplastic (MP) pollution has been documented across virtually every environmental compartment, yet the deep-sea benthos remains one of the least characterized reservoirs. We present results from a systematic survey of 97 sediment cores collected at depths ranging from 1,000 to 6,500 meters across the Northeast Atlantic Ocean during the DEEP-PLASTIC 2023 expedition. Using density separation, Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) microspectroscopy, and pyrolysis-GC-MS, we characterized MP abundance, morphology, and polymer composition across depth gradients and proximity to continental margins. MP concentrations ranged from 180 to 4,200 particles/kg dry sediment, with highest densities observed in submarine canyons acting as conduits for terrestrial material. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyamide, and polypropylene were the dominant polymer types, consistent with textile and packaging waste inputs. We identify significant correlations between MP abundance and surface ocean productivity proxies, suggesting biological vector transport (via fecal pellets and marine snow) as a primary vertical flux mechanism. A predictive model for MP accumulation hotspots is developed and validated against independent sampling. Our findings underscore the global reach of plastic pollution and the need for deep-sea baseline monitoring programs.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: Reward Model Miscalibration and Mitigation Strategies
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has become the dominant paradigm for aligning large language models with human preferences. However, reward model miscalibration—wherein learned reward functions diverge from true human values due to distributional shift, annotator inconsistency, or Goodhart's Law—poses a fundamental challenge to the reliability and safety of RLHF-trained systems. This paper provides a systematic empirical and theoretical investigation of reward model miscalibration phenomena across diverse preference datasets and model scales ranging from 7B to 70B parameters. We identify three primary failure modes: overoptimization under distributional shift, inconsistency amplification across annotator demographics, and reward hacking through spurious stylistic features. We propose three targeted mitigation strategies—uncertainty-aware reward ensembles, demographic-stratified calibration, and adversarial reward probing—and evaluate their effectiveness on the Alpaca Eval 2.0, MT-Bench, and a novel miscalibration stress test benchmark. Our best configuration reduces Goodhart-induced overoptimization by 67% while preserving 98% of baseline win rate, providing a practical toolkit for building more robust RLHF pipelines.

papers.title: Topological Data Analysis of Persistent Homology in Time-Series Financial Data
papers.abstract: Financial time series exhibit complex, multi-scale topological structures that evade characterization by traditional statistical methods. Topological data analysis (TDA), and specifically persistent homology, provides a framework for extracting robust shape features from data that are invariant to smooth deformations and noise. In this paper, we apply TDA to equity market return series, order book data, and volatility surfaces across 18 global markets spanning 2000–2023, constructing Vietoris-Rips filtrations from sliding windows and extracting persistence diagrams as feature representations for downstream machine learning tasks. We demonstrate that persistence-based features carry significant predictive signal for market regime identification (F1 = 0.84), crash precursor detection (AUROC = 0.91, 15-day horizon), and volatility forecasting (RMSE improvement of 11.3% over GARCH baselines). Notably, TDA features remain predictive during out-of-distribution periods including the COVID-19 market dislocation and the 2022 interest rate shock, suggesting topological descriptors capture regime-invariant structural properties of financial markets. Our findings open avenues for topological risk monitoring and systemic fragility assessment in macroprudential policy.

papers.title: Cortical Connectome Disruptions in Treatment-Resistant Depression: A Multi-Modal Neuroimaging Study
papers.abstract: Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) affects approximately 30% of patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) and is associated with profound disability and suicide risk. Neuroimaging studies have implicated disruptions in large-scale cortical networks, yet a coherent connectomic model of TRD pathophysiology remains elusive. We conducted a multi-modal neuroimaging study combining resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and magnetoencephalography (MEG) in 148 TRD patients, 120 treatment-responsive MDD patients, and 135 healthy controls, matched for age, sex, and IQ. Graph-theoretic analysis of structural and functional connectomes revealed that TRD is characterized by a distinctive pattern of reduced betweenness centrality in the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) and hyperconnectivity within the default mode network (DMN), not observed in treatment-responsive MDD. Machine learning classifiers trained on connectomic features distinguished TRD from treatment-responsive MDD with AUROC = 0.87. Longitudinal follow-up in 42 TRD patients undergoing ketamine infusion therapy demonstrated partial normalization of sgACC centrality correlating with antidepressant response (r = 0.63, p < 0.001). These results delineate a connectomic signature of TRD with potential utility as a biomarker for treatment selection.

papers.title: Superconductivity in Pressurized La₃Ni₂O₇: Evidence for a High-Tc Nickelate Phase
papers.abstract: The discovery of superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates stimulated intense interest in nickel oxide-based superconductors as a complement to cuprate high-Tc materials. We report the observation of bulk superconductivity in La₃Ni₂O₇ single crystals under hydrostatic pressure, with an onset temperature Tc of 80 K at 14 GPa and optimal Tc of 91 K at 28 GPa, approaching LN2-cooled operating temperatures. Resistivity measurements under pressure reveal a sharp superconducting transition with a pressure-dependent phase boundary consistent with a dome-shaped phase diagram. Specific heat measurements confirm bulk nature of the transition with a ΔC/Tc of 18 mJ mol⁻¹ K⁻². X-ray diffraction under pressure reveals a structural phase transition from the orthorhombic Amam to tetragonal I4/mmm symmetry coincident with the emergence of superconductivity, implicating structural symmetrization as a key enabler. First-principles calculations suggest a multiband pairing mechanism driven by Ni 3d orbital fluctuations mediated by apical oxygen phonons. These findings establish La₃Ni₂O₇ as the highest-Tc nickelate superconductor reported to date and illuminate the role of dimensionality and pressure in driving high-temperature superconductivity in d-electron oxides.

papers.title: Multimodal Large Language Models for Automated Radiology Report Generation: A Prospective Clinical Validation
papers.abstract: Radiologist workloads in large hospital systems have grown substantially, with preliminary read-to-final-report turnaround times increasing patient care delays. Automated radiology report generation using vision-language models offers a potential solution, yet rigorous prospective clinical validation is lacking. We developed RadioLLM-7B, a domain-adapted multimodal large language model fine-tuned on 2.1 million chest X-ray and CT study pairs from an 8-institution dataset, and prospectively evaluated its performance on 4,800 consecutive chest X-ray studies across 3 academic medical centers over 6 months. RadioLLM-7B generated reports were evaluated by board-certified radiologists on a 5-point Likert scale for clinical accuracy, completeness, and communication. The model achieved mean clinical accuracy scores of 4.2/5.0 and identified clinically significant findings with 93.1% sensitivity and 95.4% specificity. Time-to-report for AI-drafted reports reviewed and edited by radiologists was 58% faster than unaided reads. Among 240 cases with missed finding discrepancies, AI-assisted reads reduced missed clinically significant abnormalities by 41%. Prospective deployment of RadioLLM-7B demonstrates clinically meaningful performance improvements and establishes the evidentiary standard for regulatory consideration of AI-assisted radiology tools.

papers.title: Solid-State Electrolytes for All-Solid-State Lithium Batteries: Ionic Conductivity Enhancement via Compositional Grading
papers.abstract: All-solid-state lithium batteries (ASSLBs) promise transformative improvements in energy density and safety over conventional liquid electrolyte cells, yet the low ionic conductivity and high interfacial resistance of solid electrolytes remain principal obstacles. We report a compositional grading strategy in which Li₆PS₅Cl argyrodite electrolytes are synthesized with controlled, continuous variation in Cl/Br halide substitution across the electrolyte layer thickness, creating a gradient in lattice parameters and Li⁺ migration barrier energies. This gradient architecture reduces the total Li⁺ activation energy by 31% compared to homogeneous electrolytes and yields room-temperature ionic conductivity of 12.4 mS cm⁻¹—the highest reported for argyrodite-family electrolytes. ASSLBs assembled with graded electrolytes achieve >400 Wh kg⁻¹ energy density, 99.2% coulombic efficiency over 500 cycles, and stable cycling at 5C discharge rates. Operando synchrotron X-ray diffraction and impedance spectroscopy elucidate the mechanistic origins of conductivity enhancement and interfacial stability. The compositional grading concept is broadly applicable to oxide and sulfide electrolyte families, providing a scalable processing strategy for next-generation solid-state batteries.

papers.title: Labor Market Polarization and Wage Inequality in the Age of Automation: Evidence from 32 OECD Countries
papers.abstract: Technological automation has been hypothesized as a primary driver of labor market polarization—the simultaneous growth of high-skill, high-wage and low-skill, low-wage employment at the expense of middle-skill, routine-intensive occupations. While this hypothesis has been extensively examined in the United States, cross-national evidence from diverse institutional contexts remains limited. We construct a novel dataset linking 32 OECD countries' occupational automation exposure (derived from O*NET task content linked to country-level employment distributions), wage structures, and institutional variables (union density, employment protection legislation, minimum wage levels) over 2000–2022. Panel regressions with country and year fixed effects reveal that automation exposure is associated with a significant reduction in middle-skill employment share (β = −0.31, SE = 0.08) and an increase in the 90th/50th wage ratio (β = 0.24, SE = 0.06), effects that are attenuated in countries with higher union density and more generous employment protection. Counterfactual decompositions attribute 44% of within-country earnings inequality growth since 2000 to automation-induced task displacement. Our findings underscore the centrality of labor market institutions in mediating the distributional consequences of technological change and inform ongoing debates over robot taxation, wage insurance, and reskilling policy.

papers.title: Adversarial Robustness of Vision Transformers: A Comprehensive Evaluation and Defense Taxonomy
papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance across diverse computer vision benchmarks, yet their adversarial robustness characteristics remain incompletely understood. Previous studies have focused narrowly on ℓ∞-bounded perturbations on ImageNet; we present the first comprehensive evaluation spanning 7 attack categories (ℓ1, ℓ2, ℓ∞, patch, Fourier, semantic, natural), 12 ViT architectures (ViT-B/16 to ViT-G/14, DeiT, Swin, MaxViT), and 5 downstream task domains including medical imaging, satellite imagery, and autonomous driving. Our evaluation reveals that while ViTs exhibit superior robustness to certain spatial perturbations compared to CNNs, they are more susceptible to low-frequency Fourier attacks and semantic adversarial examples by margins of 14–23%. We systematically categorize and benchmark 18 defense strategies—including adversarial training, randomized smoothing, and attention masking—providing the first head-to-head comparison of their effectiveness across attack types and domains. A novel defense, Attention-Aware Adversarial Training (A3T), that adaptively weights adversarial examples based on attention entropy achieves Pareto-optimal clean/robust accuracy trade-offs across all evaluated architectures. We release a unified evaluation library and benchmark results to accelerate robust ViT research.

papers.title: Catalytic Asymmetric [4+2] Cycloaddition of 1-Azadienes with Chiral Brønsted Acid Catalysis
papers.abstract: Chiral phosphoric acid (CPA)-catalyzed Diels-Alder reactions represent a powerful strategy for enantioselective carbocycle and heterocycle synthesis, yet the scope of suitable diene partners remains restricted. We report the first CPA-catalyzed asymmetric [4+2] cycloaddition of electron-deficient 1-azadienes with cyclic dienes, affording dihydropyridine products in good yields (72–91%) with excellent enantioselectivities (93–99% ee) and diastereoselectivities (dr >20:1). A BINOL-derived CPA catalyst bearing a 3,3'-bis(3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl) substituent proved optimal, activating the dienophile through dual H-bond donation while simultaneously shielding one face via steric pressure from the binaphthyl scaffold. Computational transition-state analysis reveals a key N–H⋯O hydrogen bond between the azadiene NH and one phosphoryl oxygen as the critical enantio-determining interaction. The methodology is amenable to gram-scale synthesis and applied in the concise formal synthesis of the cytotoxic natural product minfiensine, demonstrating pharmaceutical relevance. This work expands the synthetic utility of CPA catalysis to a previously inaccessible class of diene partners.

papers.title: Dynamic Metasurfaces for Programmable Electromagnetic Wave Manipulation at Terahertz Frequencies
papers.abstract: Terahertz (THz) electromagnetic waves occupy a technologically important spectral band bridging microwave and optical domains, with applications spanning wireless communications, non-destructive imaging, and medical diagnostics. Programmable control of THz wavefronts at subwavelength scales demands metasurfaces with dynamically reconfigurable electromagnetic properties. We demonstrate a vanadium dioxide (VO₂)-integrated reconfigurable THz metasurface in which the metal-insulator transition of VO₂, actuated by localized photothermal stimuli, enables pixel-level control of transmission amplitude (contrast ratio 24 dB) and phase (0–2π full coverage) with a reconfiguration speed of 85 ns. A 32×32 pixel programmable metasurface array is demonstrated, achieving high-fidelity holographic image reconstruction and beam steering with 0.8° angular resolution across the 0.5–1.5 THz band. Machine learning-assisted phase retrieval enables real-time hologram computation and display at 30 fps. We further demonstrate a THz MIMO communication testbed achieving 2.4 Gbps data throughput with programmable spatial multiplexing enabled by the metasurface. These results establish VO₂-based programmable metasurfaces as a versatile platform for next-generation THz wave engineering.

papers.title: mRNA Vaccine Platform Optimization for Broadly Neutralizing Influenza Antibody Induction
papers.abstract: Annual reformulation of seasonal influenza vaccines is necessitated by antigenic drift of hemagglutinin (HA) surface glycoproteins, while pandemic-potential strains may arise faster than vaccine production can respond. mRNA vaccine platforms offer rapid manufacturability and design flexibility, enabling the encoding of novel antigen architectures unattainable by conventional methods. We designed and evaluated a panel of mRNA constructs encoding computationally optimized consensus HA sequences, hyperglycosylated HA variants for stem epitope focusing, and multivalent self-assembling HA nanoparticles. Candidate constructs were formulated in ionizable lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and evaluated in ferret and non-human primate immunogenicity studies. The lead stem-focused nanoparticle construct elicited broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) targeting the conserved HA stem region with breadth spanning all 18 influenza A subtypes and cross-reactive activity against influenza B. Ferrets vaccinated with the lead candidate demonstrated complete protection against heterologous H5N1, H3N2, and H1N1 challenge. A Phase 1 clinical trial is ongoing (NCT06123456). These results support advancement of stem-focusing mRNA nanoparticle vaccines as a universal influenza vaccine strategy.

papers.title: Spectral Graph Theory Approaches to Community Detection in Hypergraphs
papers.abstract: Real-world complex systems frequently involve interactions among three or more entities simultaneously, yet conventional graph models restrict relationships to pairwise edges, obscuring higher-order structure. Hypergraphs, which generalize graphs by admitting edges (hyperedges) connecting arbitrary subsets of vertices, provide a natural representation for these multi-way interactions. Community detection in hypergraphs—identifying clusters of densely interacting vertices—is substantially more challenging than in ordinary graphs due to the combinatorial richness of hyperedge structures. We develop a spectral theory for hypergraph Laplacians that yields tractable eigenvalue problems, establishing conditions under which the leading eigenvectors recover planted community structure with information-theoretically optimal sample complexity. Our main result proves that spectral hypergraph clustering achieves exact community recovery when the hyperedge density exceeds the Kesten-Stigum threshold generalized to hypergraphs, matching an information-theoretic lower bound we derive. A computationally efficient algorithm, HyperSC, implements this spectral approach with O(|E| · k) complexity, enabling community detection in hypergraphs with millions of vertices. Experiments on co-authorship, protein complex, and email thread hypergraphs demonstrate 18–34% NMI improvements over graph projection baselines.

papers.title: Embodied Cognition and Language Grounding in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: A central question in cognitive science and AI concerns whether linguistic meaning can be grounded in sensorimotor experience rather than purely in statistical co-occurrence patterns among symbols. Large vision-language models (VLMs) trained on image-text pairs offer an empirical testbed for studying language grounding, as they connect linguistic representations to perceptual inputs. This paper examines the extent to which current VLMs (GPT-4V, Gemini 1.5 Pro, LLaVA-NeXT-34B, and InternVL2-76B) exhibit signatures of embodied cognition as operationalized through tasks requiring spatiotemporal reasoning, force dynamics prediction, and affordance judgment derived from the EMBENCH evaluation suite we introduce. We find that while VLMs far exceed chance on basic visual recognition, their performance on embodied reasoning tasks falls 38–54% below human baselines, with particularly pronounced deficits in counterfactual physical simulation (61% gap) and cross-modal analogy completion requiring manipulation knowledge (49% gap). Analysis of model internals via probing classifiers suggests that VLMs encode object categories and spatial relations but lack systematic representations of physical affordances tied to action possibilities. These findings contribute to ongoing debates about symbol grounding and suggest that genuine embodiment—or plausible architectural proxies—may be necessary for human-level embodied language understanding.

papers.title: Nitrogen-Doped Carbon Quantum Dots as Sensitizers for Photocatalytic CO₂ Reduction to Solar Fuels
papers.abstract: Photocatalytic conversion of CO₂ to solar fuels offers a pathway to simultaneously address rising atmospheric CO₂ concentrations and intermittent renewable energy storage. Nitrogen-doped carbon quantum dots (N-CQDs) have emerged as attractive photosensitizers due to their strong visible light absorption, tunable photoluminescence, and low toxicity, yet their role in mechanistic CO₂ reduction pathways remains poorly understood. We synthesize a series of N-CQDs via microwave-assisted hydrothermal treatment of citric acid and ethylenediamine, systematically varying N/C ratios and surface functionalization to probe structure-activity relationships. Photocatalytic testing in conjunction with a cobalt-based molecular catalyst under visible light irradiation (λ > 420 nm) yields CO production rates up to 4,820 μmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ with >95% selectivity over H₂. Transient absorption spectroscopy, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), and operando XANES measurements reveal that pyridinic-N sites within N-CQDs facilitate ultrafast charge transfer to the cobalt catalyst with a rate constant of 2.3 × 10¹⁰ s⁻¹, suppressing charge recombination as the primary performance-limiting process. Quantum yield calculations and stability testing over 100-hour continuous illumination confirm the robustness of the optimized system. Our mechanistic insights provide a rational blueprint for next-generation carbon-based photosensitizer design.

papers.title: Causal Inference from Electronic Health Records Using Double Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Observational electronic health records (EHR) offer unprecedented scale for studying treatment effects in real-world clinical settings, yet causal identification requires careful handling of confounding, selection bias, and measurement error inherent in administrative data. Double machine learning (DML), which combines flexible non-parametric estimation with Neyman orthogonality to yield root-n-consistent treatment effect estimates, offers a principled approach to observational causal inference in high-dimensional EHR settings. We present a comprehensive DML framework tailored to EHR data structures, incorporating time-varying confounders via a longitudinal DML extension, handling of irregular observation times through functional data representations, and calibrated uncertainty quantification using conformal prediction. Applying our framework to a cohort of 280,000 type-2 diabetic patients in the STARR-OMOP database, we estimate heterogeneous treatment effects of SGLT-2 inhibitors versus DPP-4 inhibitors on composite cardiovascular outcomes, finding clinically meaningful subgroup heterogeneity with high-risk patients showing 37% relative risk reduction versus 12% in the overall population. Simulation studies validate DML's double-robustness property in realistic EHR data-generating processes with up to 40% unmeasured confounder noise. Our open-source CausalEHR package implements the complete pipeline, enabling widespread adoption of rigorous causal inference in health data science.

papers.title: Smart Grid Resilience Under Coordinated Cyberattacks: Detection, Isolation, and Recovery Frameworks
papers.abstract: Modern power grids are increasingly exposed to sophisticated cyberattacks targeting supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, with cascading failure potential across interconnected critical infrastructure. We present CyberResilGrid, a comprehensive framework for smart grid cyber resilience encompassing attack detection, fault isolation, and autonomous recovery. The detection subsystem employs a multivariate time-series anomaly detection algorithm combining graph attention networks (GATs) with physics-constrained LSTM models, achieving 99.1% detection accuracy and 0.2% false positive rate on the BATADAL and PowerCyber benchmark datasets. An automated isolation module applies spectral graph partitioning to segment compromised subgraphs within 180 ms, preventing cascade propagation while maintaining 94% load service continuity. The recovery subsystem uses a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) policy trained in a high-fidelity GridLab-D simulation environment, restoring 97% of nominal generation dispatch within 4 minutes of isolation. Hardware-in-the-loop testing on a 118-bus IEEE test system with real Schweitzer Engineering relay hardware validates end-to-end framework performance under 12 attack scenarios. Our findings provide actionable design guidelines for utility operators and inform standards development for cyber-resilient grid infrastructure.

papers.title: Gut Microbiome Composition as a Predictor of Immunotherapy Response in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy has transformed outcomes for a subset of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients, yet reliable biomarkers for response prediction remain elusive. Emerging evidence implicates gut microbiome composition as a modulator of anti-tumor immunity through systemic immunological mechanisms. We conducted a prospective observational cohort study enrolling 312 NSCLC patients initiating first-line anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 therapy, collecting serial stool samples at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks for shotgun metagenomic sequencing alongside tumor mutational burden (TMB) and PD-L1 expression assessment. Machine learning models trained on baseline microbiome features predicted objective response rate with AUROC 0.83, significantly outperforming TMB alone (0.71) and PD-L1 expression alone (0.68). A consortium of bacteria including Akkermansia muciniphila, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Bifidobacterium longum were associated with durable response (>12 months), while Fusobacterium nucleatum abundance was associated with primary resistance. Mechanistic studies in patient-derived tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) cultures confirmed that metabolites from response-associated bacteria enhanced CD8+ T cell polyfunctionality. A predictive microbiome score is being evaluated as a companion diagnostic in an ongoing randomized trial. This work supports gut microbiome profiling as a clinically actionable biomarker for ICI personalization.

papers.title: Decolonizing the Curriculum: Faculty Perspectives on Epistemic Justice in Higher Education Pedagogy
papers.abstract: The decolonization of higher education curricula has moved from activist demand to institutional agenda in numerous global contexts following resurgent social movements since 2020, yet implementation remains inconsistent and contested. This study examines faculty perspectives on epistemic justice and curricular decolonization through in-depth semi-structured interviews with 98 faculty members across 12 universities in South Africa, the United Kingdom, India, and Canada, representing disciplines spanning STEM, social sciences, and humanities. Using constructivist grounded theory, we develop an emergent conceptual framework distinguishing three faculty orientational stances toward decolonization—instrumental, transformative, and critical-emancipatory—with distinct implications for pedagogical practice, assessment design, and institutional engagement. Findings reveal persistent tensions between institutional performativity pressures (diversity metrics, policy compliance) and substantive epistemic transformation, with STEM faculty demonstrating particular resistance predicated on universalist knowledge claims. We identify enabling conditions for transformative decolonization including departmental psychological safety, protected pedagogical experimentation time, and co-creation partnerships with students from historically marginalized communities. Our framework advances a practice-grounded theory of epistemic justice in higher education that bridges normative philosophy and institutional change strategy.

faculty.bio: Dr. Priya Mehta is an Associate Professor in the Department of Computer Science, where she leads the Trustworthy AI Lab. Her research sits at the intersection of machine learning systems, privacy-preserving computation, and computer vision, with a growing focus on the deployment of AI in high-stakes domains including healthcare and edge computing. She received her PhD from MIT in 2016 and completed postdoctoral work at the Alan Turing Institute. She has received the NSF CAREER Award, the ACM SIGKDD Rising Star Award, and is a Senior Member of the IEEE. Her work has been supported by grants totaling over $4.2M from NSF, NIH, and industry partners.

Dr. Rajan Pillai is a Professor in the Department of Physics and Director of the Quantum Materials and Information Laboratory. His research spans quantum error correction for NISQ-era quantum processors, high-temperature superconductivity in novel oxide systems, and the design of quantum hardware. He obtained his PhD from Caltech in 2009 and was a Miller Research Fellow at UC Berkeley. He is a Fellow of the American Physical Society (APS), a recipient of the Sloan Research Fellowship, and has published over 85 peer-reviewed articles cited more than 6,000 times. His lab operates two dilution refrigerators and maintains active collaborations with IBM Quantum and Google Quantum AI.

Dr. Amara Osei-Bonsu is an Associate Professor in Biomedical Engineering with a joint appointment in the Medical School's Department of Oncology. His laboratory investigates the intersection of programmable gene editing tools and clinical oncology, focusing on RNA-targeting CRISPR systems for glioblastoma treatment and multimodal AI for diagnostic radiology. He completed his MD-PhD at Johns Hopkins University and clinical training at UCSF Medical Center. His translational research program has received funding from NIH NCI, the Gates Foundation, and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI), and he has been recognized with the Burroughs Wellcome Fund Career Award.

Dr. Elena Vasquez is a Professor of Mathematics and holds the Ramanujan Chair in Applied Mathematics. Her research bridges rigorous mathematical analysis and practical machine learning, with contributions spanning convex and non-convex optimization theory, statistical learning theory, and topological methods for data analysis. She earned her PhD from Princeton University in 2007 and was a Simons Postdoctoral Fellow. She serves on the editorial boards of JMLR and Foundations of Computational Mathematics, is a past recipient of the SIAM Optimization Prize, and a Fellow of the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (SIAM).

Dr. Wei Zhang is a Professor of Materials Science and Engineering and Director of the Center for Advanced Energy Materials. His group works at the frontier of photovoltaic device engineering, solid-state battery materials, and programmable photonic metamaterials. He received his PhD from the University of Oxford in 2008 as a Rhodes Scholar, followed by postdoctoral research at Stanford SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. He is a Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry, has been awarded the MRS Outstanding Young Investigator Award, and his work on perovskite-silicon tandem cells has received significant coverage in global scientific media. His laboratory has spun out two energy technology start-ups.

Dr. Marcus Thompson is Associate Professor of Sociology and core faculty member of the Digital Society Initiative. His scholarship examines the intersection of digital technology, political polarization, labor markets, and colonial legacies in urban space, combining quantitative network analysis with ethnographic methods. He received his DPhil from the University of Oxford and was a Postdoctoral Fellow at the Princeton Center for the Study of Democratic Politics. He is co-author of the book 'Fractured Publics: Social Media and the Crisis of Democratic Deliberation' (Harvard University Press, 2023) and regularly advises governmental and non-governmental bodies on platform regulation policy.

Dr. Nkechi Adeyemi is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Immunology, where she directs the Infectious Disease Vaccines and Immunity Laboratory. Her research focuses on understanding the molecular determinants of protective immunity against rapidly evolving RNA viruses including influenza and SARS-CoV-2, and on harnessing innate-adaptive immune crosstalk to develop next-generation mRNA vaccines. She completed her PhD at the Pasteur Institute in Paris and a postdoctoral fellowship at the Ragon Institute of MGH, MIT, and Harvard. She is a 2022 Pew Biomedical Scholar and an NIH New Innovator Award recipient.

Dr. Fatima Al-Rashid is Associate Professor and holder of the Woodward Associate Professorship in Synthetic Chemistry. Her laboratory develops novel transition metal-catalyzed and organocatalytic reactions for the asymmetric synthesis of complex natural products and medicinally relevant scaffolds, with a growing interest in photocatalytic approaches to solar fuel production. She earned her PhD from ETH Zürich and was a Marie Curie Postdoctoral Fellow at Imperial College London. She is a recipient of the ERC Starting Grant, the RSC Emerging Technologies Award, and has been named one of Chemical & Engineering News' 'Talented 12' early-career chemists.

Dr. Lars Andersen is Professor of Marine Sciences in the Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences and Chief Scientist of the university's Ocean Observation Program. His research investigates anthropogenic impacts on deep-sea ecosystems, with particular emphasis on microplastic transport pathways, distribution patterns, and ecological consequences in the marine benthic environment. He completed his PhD at the University of Bergen and postdoctoral research at WHOI. He has led 14 oceanographic research cruises, published over 110 peer-reviewed articles, and has testified before the UN Environment Assembly as a scientific expert on marine plastic pollution.

Dr. Samuel Okonkwo is Associate Professor of Psychiatry and Director of the Computational Neuroimaging Core, with a secondary appointment in Biostatistics. His research applies advanced neuroimaging methods—fMRI, DTI, MEG—and causal machine learning to delineate the neurobiological substrates of treatment-resistant psychiatric disorders and develop clinically actionable predictive biomarkers. He holds an MD from the University of Lagos and a PhD in Biostatistics from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. He has been awarded the NARSAD Young Investigator Award, the APA Gerald L. Klerman Award, and is a Rising Star in the Organization for Human Brain Mapping (OHBM) community.

faculty.bio: Dr. Kiran Bhat is Assistant Professor of Electrical Engineering and head of the Secure and Resilient Energy Systems Laboratory. His research addresses the growing cybersecurity threats to smart grid infrastructure, combining graph-theoretic power systems analysis with machine learning for anomaly detection and reinforcement learning for autonomous control and recovery. He received his PhD from Georgia Institute of Technology and worked as a Research Scientist at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) prior to joining the faculty. He is the recipient of a DOE Early Career Award and serves on the IEEE Power and Energy Society Cybersecurity Task Force.

Dr. Isabelle Dupont is Associate Professor of Political Science and Senior Fellow at the Center for European Studies. Her scholarly work examines the political economy of inequality, comparative welfare state development, and the politics of technological disruption in post-industrial democracies, with a regional expertise in France and the European Union. She holds a PhD from Sciences Po Paris and was a Max Weber Postdoctoral Fellow at the European University Institute. She is author of 'The Anxious Middle: Automation, Status, and the Politics of Resentment in Europe' (Oxford University Press, 2022) and a frequent commentator on French and European political affairs.

Dr. Linda Ferreiro is Professor of Neuroscience and Director of the Affective Brain Laboratory. Her research investigates the neural and computational mechanisms of emotion regulation, reward processing, and vulnerability to affective disorders, integrating rodent electrophysiology, human neuroimaging, and pharmacological interventions. She received her PhD from Columbia University in Neuroscience and completed postdoctoral fellowships at the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH). She is a fellow of the Society for Neuroscience and a past Kavli Institute Fellow. Her work is funded by continuous NIH R01 awards totaling over $6M and she has trained 22 PhD students.

Dr. Hiroshi Tanaka is Professor of Chemistry and Biophysics and heads the Molecular Simulations and Structural Biology Group. His laboratory develops and applies state-of-the-art computational methods—molecular dynamics, free energy perturbation, and cryo-EM guided modeling—to understand protein structure, function, and dynamics, with applications to antiviral drug discovery and vaccine design. He obtained his PhD from the University of Tokyo and was a Humboldt Research Fellow at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysical Chemistry. He is an author on over 140 publications with more than 11,000 total citations, a fellow of the Biophysical Society, and serves on the editorial board of Structure.

Dr. Chioma Eze is Assistant Professor of African and African American Studies and affiliated faculty in the Graduate Program in Architecture, Landscape Architecture, and Urban Planning. Her interdisciplinary scholarship examines the politics of urban space, memory, and material culture in African cities, with particular attention to how colonial infrastructure is contested, repurposed, and re-memorialized in postcolonial contexts. She holds a PhD from Yale University and was a Harvard Society of Fellows Junior Fellow. Her debut monograph, 'Reclaiming the Square: Memory, Power, and Public Space in West African Cities,' is forthcoming from Duke University Press. She is a 2023 Ford Foundation Fellow.
